design_detail: Review of human studies of cocaine and cognition with a stated PubMed search, in two parts: 14 placebo-controlled laboratory studies of acute cocaine administration (narrative synthesis only, Table 2) and 61 case–control studies published from 2003 onwards comparing people with a history of cocaine use with non-drug or non-cocaine-using controls (narrative synthesis by cognitive domain, Table 3, plus eight random-effects meta-analyses of standardized mean differences on subsets of three to nine studies). Domains: attention, response inhibition, memory and learning, cognitive flexibility, performance monitoring, reward-based decision making, psychomotor performance. Read from the uncorrected proof, not the version of record.
can_establish: How large the reported test-score differences were, domain by domain, between people with a history of cocaine use (mostly people with cocaine dependence) and control groups in the cross-sectional studies the authors pooled up to about 2013, and which cognitive domains had any placebo-controlled data on acute effects.
cannot_establish: That cocaine caused the differences (every long-term study is cross-sectional, with no pre-use measurement and no adjustment for education, other drugs or premorbid ability); that the differences amount to impairment (no comparison with norms); how results change with abstinence or with recreational versus dependent use (no moderator analyses); that the pooled estimates are unbiased (one database, no risk-of-bias or publication-bias assessment, studies removed for heterogeneity); or what acute cocaine does to cognition in people without prior use.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (review). Studies were found by a PubMed search combining cocaine with cognition, cognitive or neuropsychology, and with each domain term, limited to humans and adults, plus a check of reference lists; English only; no search dates and no flow of records are given (§2.1, PDF pp. 2–3).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Acute studies: placebo-controlled laboratory administration of cocaine. Long-term studies: people with a history of recreational use, abuse or dependence compared with a non-drug or non-cocaine-using control group free of medical and psychiatric disorders, published from 2003 onwards because studies from 1987–2002 had been reviewed by Jovanovski et al. (2005). Meta-analyses: at least three studies reporting N, means and SDs on an outcome judged representative of the domain; behavioural results from fMRI studies left out (§2.1–2.2, PDF pp. 2–3).
sample.demographics: Not summarized. Tables 2 and 3 give group sizes, a description of each sample's use (dependence, abuse, recreational use, crack use), frequency and years of use, and abstinence where reported; age, sex and education are not tabulated (PDF pp. 5–9).
sample.selection_effects: Single-database, English-only search without stated dates or a record of screening. Long-term samples are mostly people with cocaine dependence; the authors note that only a minority of studies examined people who use cocaine recreationally (§4.5, PDF p. 16). Every acute study tested people with previous cocaine experience, most with dependence or crack use and several within 72 hours of last use (Table 2, PDF p. 5), so the acute results do not describe people without prior use, as the authors acknowledge (§4.3, PDF p. 15). Table 3 also lists two long-term studies published before the 2003 cut-off (Fillmore, 2002; Kirby et al., 1999).

exposure.measurement: As reported by the primary studies. The review tabulates diagnostic category, frequency and total years of use and abstinence, with many entries marked unknown (Table 3, PDF pp. 6–9). In the acute studies cocaine or placebo was given in the laboratory (Table 2, PDF p. 5).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Acute studies: intravenous, oral, intranasal and smoked administration, several doses per study; doses appear in Table 2 as study conditions and are not reproduced here. Long-term studies: frequency entries range from under about 3 occasions a month (recreational samples) to several days a week, and duration up to about 21 years of use; many entries are unknown (Table 3).
exposure.polysubstance: Not handled in the analyses. The authors state that most if not all participants in the reviewed studies used several drugs and suggest controls with similar use of other drugs but no cocaine (§4.3, PDF p. 15). Examples in Table 3: a cocaine-dependent sample with and without alcohol use (Abi-Saab et al., 2005) and a sample dependent on two or more substances (Tanabe et al., 2009, footnote f).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Acute studies: from under 72 hours to weeks before the sessions, or a negative urine test (Table 2). Long-term studies: from under 72 hours, or cocaine-positive urine at screening, to months or years, and often unknown; by the editors' count about 23 of the 55 distinct study labels in Table 3 included at least some participants tested within 72 hours of last use or with positive urine. No analysis by abstinence was possible (§4.4, PDF p. 16).

comparison.controls: Acute studies: placebo sessions in the same participants. Long-term studies: non-drug or non-cocaine-using controls free of medical and psychiatric disorders; in some studies the controls used other drugs but not cocaine (for example the polydrug controls of Colzato, 2009a, Table 3).
comparison.matching: Not extracted or assessed by the review.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No study measured cognition before cocaine use. The authors state that group differences can never be read as caused solely by cocaine, that people who use cocaine may differ beforehand in cognition and personality, and that education and lifestyle are major potential confounders (§4.3, PDF p. 15).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Varied and not tabulated; non-cocaine-using controls could use other drugs.

outcomes.instruments: Paradigms by domain (Table 1, PDF p. 4): attention (P300, CPT, IMT, RVIP, Stroop, Cocaine Stroop, Global–Local task and others); response inhibition (stop-signal task, Go/NoGo, IMT); memory (CVLT, RAVLT, LMT, HVLT, n-back, digit span, spatial working memory); stimulus–response learning; cognitive flexibility (WCST, IED, reversal learning); performance monitoring (ERN, Pe, post-error slowing); reward-based decision making (delay discounting, IGT, BART); psychomotor performance (DSST, Trail Making, finger tapping, grooved pegboard).
outcomes.validity_norms: No comparison with normative data; every result is a difference from a control group.
outcomes.operationalization: Impairment means poorer performance than the control group, either a statistically significant difference in a primary study or a pooled standardized mean difference graded small (0.2 or less), moderate (about 0.5) or large (about 0.8 or more) (§2.2, PDF p. 3).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None for the eight pooled outcomes or for the many narrative comparisons.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable to the review; not extracted for the primary studies.

analysis.effect_sizes: Random-effects standardized mean differences with 95% CIs (RevMan 5.2.2), long-term studies only; I² is said to have been computed but is not reported for any pool; no prediction intervals, per-study estimates or forest plots. Sustained attention (CPT hits with P300 amplitude) −1.22 (−1.58 to −0.85), number of studies not stated; stop-signal reaction time 0.50 (0.11 to 0.90), 3 studies; failed inhibitions (commission errors) 0.64 (0.44 to 0.84), 9 studies stated, 8 named; immediate recall −0.46 (−0.70 to −0.23), 8 studies; perseverative errors 0.37 (0.17 to 0.57), 5 studies; reward-based decision making (delay-discounting k and IGT net score) 0.53 (0.32 to 0.75), 7 studies; psychomotor motor responses 0.75 (0.46 to 1.04), 3 studies; psychomotor response time −0.24 (−0.47 to −0.02), 6 studies. All are in the direction of poorer performance in the cocaine groups; the sign convention differs between outcomes. Studies were removed for their contribution to heterogeneity in the attention, stop-signal, perseveration and motor-response pools. No acute pooling (too few comparable studies).
analysis.covariates: None; unadjusted group means and SDs were pooled.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Studies were dropped post hoc from four of the eight pools because they contributed to heterogeneity, including studies with null results (Liu et al., 2011, attention; Woicik et al., 2009, finger tapping); the studies in the attention pool are not identified, nor which three stop-signal and which five perseveration studies were kept; participant totals per pool are not given. Several counts in the text disagree with the studies named or with Tables 2 and 3 (see reporting issues).
analysis.power: Not addressed. The acute studies had 8 to 48 participants each (editors' count: 13 of 14 had 14 or fewer); the long-term pools rest on three to nine small cross-sectional studies, and the authors call the number of studies per analysis very small (§4.4, PDF p. 16).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Eight pooled standardized differences between cocaine groups and controls, 0.24 to 1.22 in absolute size, each from three to nine cross-sectional studies, with studies dropped for heterogeneity in four pools and no information on heterogeneity, study-level bias or publication bias; narratively, poorer performance of cocaine groups in most domains alongside several null studies. The 14 acute studies (8 to 48 people with previous cocaine use each) found better inhibition in three of four studies and faster DSST responding in two of six, and mostly no effect elsewhere.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract describes long-term use as “characterized by a general cognitive impairment across functions” (PDF p. 1), and the domain summaries use causal wording (cocaine worsening immediate recall, long-term use having an impairing effect on perseveration, chronic cocaine having a relatively large impact on psychomotor performance; PDF pp. 11, 12, 14) without norms, adjustment for confounding or a pre-use baseline. The response-inhibition summary says every reviewed study points to impairment, although the same section reports two non-significant stop-signal studies and a null study with a composite measure (PDF pp. 10–11). The abstract presents acute enhancement of response inhibition and psychomotor speed, while §4.3 warns that this may only offset pre-existing deficits in people who regularly use cocaine (PDF p. 15), and it offers atherosclerosis as a possible mechanism that the review does not examine (PDF pp. 1, 14–15). The causal caveats of §4.3 are sound but are not carried into the abstract or the domain summaries.

timeline.event: Quantitative review of studies from 1987–2002 (Jovanovski et al.); Spronk et al. start their long-term inclusion in 2003 to follow on from it and describe their long-term results as broadly in agreement with it
This review: 14 acute and 61 long-term studies, eight pooled long-term outcomes
Systematic quantitative review of cocaine and cognition including abstinence duration (Potvin et al., 2014, as cited by Frazer et al., 2018; not read)

Systematic critical review (Frazer et al.) quotes this review's abstract conclusion of general impairment and argues that its own tabulated studies do not support it, mainly because most studies lacked normative comparison, demographic matching and control of other drug use
Systematic review and meta-analysis of cocaine use and cognitive inhibition (López-Martín et al.; appraised separately)

replication.where_it_stands: Poorer average performance of people with (mostly dependent) cocaine use than controls on tests of inhibition, memory, decision making and psychomotor speed recurs across reviews (Jovanovski et al., 2005; this review). Whether the differences come from cocaine, from pre-existing differences, other drugs and alcohol, recent use or withdrawal, and whether they amount to impairment against norms, remains unsettled; Frazer et al. (2018) dispute the general-impairment reading. Acute placebo-controlled evidence is limited to small studies of people who already use cocaine.

funding.funder: ZonMW grant 31160205 to J.G. Ramaekers and R.J. Verkes; the funder had no role in study design, data collection and analysis, the decision to publish or preparation of the manuscript (Role of funding source, PDF p. 16).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors report no financial interests and no conflicts of interest (Conflicts of interest, PDF p. 16).
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Psychiatry, Radboud University Nijmegen Medical Centre, and Donders Institute (Nijmegen); Department of Neuropsychology and Psychopharmacology, Maastricht University. None of the included cocaine studies is by the review's authors; their own work is cited only for comparisons with cannabis and MDMA. Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A pre-registered systematic review searching several databases with duplicate screening, study-level risk-of-bias assessment, all eligible studies pooled with heterogeneity reported and explored rather than removed, and moderator analyses by verified abstinence, recreational versus dependent use, alcohol and other drug use and education; for causation, prospective cohorts that test cognition before regular cocaine use and repeatedly during biologically verified abstinence, scored against demographically adjusted norms. For acute effects, placebo-controlled studies that also test a matched group without cocaine use under placebo, to see whether acute improvement is a return toward the control level.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (adults with a history of cocaine use; acute: participants in placebo-controlled sessions), exposure, comparators (placebo; non-drug or non-cocaine-using controls) and cognitive outcomes are stated (§2.1, PDF pp. 2–3).
No protocol or registration is mentioned.
Placebo-controlled acute studies and case–control long-term studies are required without a stated rationale; only the 2003 cut-off is explained.
PubMed only (with reference lists), English only without justification, no search dates, no grey literature (§2.1, PDF pp. 2–3); AMSTAR 2 requires at least two databases even for a partial yes.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: No list of excluded studies and no flow of records.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Tables 2 and 3 give group sizes, type of use, frequency and years of use, abstinence, tasks and direction of results (PDF pp. 5–9), but no age, sex, education, recruitment setting or other drug use.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No risk-of-bias or quality assessment of the primary studies; confounding is discussed only in general terms (§4.3, PDF p. 15).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: Random-effects weighting is appropriate, but unadjusted means from observational studies were pooled without justification, different constructs were combined in one pool (CPT hits with P300 amplitude; delay-discounting k with IGT net score; PDF p. 3), and studies were removed post hoc because they raised heterogeneity, in four of eight pools (PDF pp. 4, 10, 12, 14).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No risk of bias was assessed, so its impact was not examined.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: §4.3 lists general sources of bias (pre-existing differences, polydrug use, education, abstinence; PDF p. 15), but study-level bias was never assessed and the domain conclusions and abstract are written causally.
I² values are never reported; heterogeneity was handled by removing studies, with only scattered task-level explanations (e.g., task difficulty in reversal learning, PDF p. 11).

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funder, its role and the absence of conflicts are stated (PDF p. 16).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Under AMSTAR 2 the review fails all seven critical items (no protocol, single-database search, no list of excluded studies, no risk-of-bias assessment, pooling with post hoc heterogeneity-based exclusions and unreported I², conclusions not tempered by study-level bias, no publication-bias assessment), which gives critically low confidence. It remains a useful map of paradigms and of the acute placebo-controlled studies up to about 2013 (Tables 1–3). Its pooled standardized differences may be cited only as summaries of selected cross-sectional group differences with these caveats, not as estimates of cocaine's effect or of clinical impairment. Its acute enhancement findings rest on small studies of people who regularly use cocaine, which the authors themselves say may reflect the offsetting of pre-existing deficits.

key_findings.finding: Search and inclusion: PubMed only, cocaine combined with cognition terms and with each domain term, limited to humans and adults, English only, plus reference lists. Acute studies had to be placebo-controlled laboratory administrations; long-term studies had to compare people with a history of recreational use, abuse or dependence with non-drug or non-cocaine-using controls free of medical and psychiatric disorders and to be published from 2003 (studies from 1987–2002 having been reviewed by Jovanovski et al., 2005). 14 acute and 61 long-term studies were included.
key_findings.locator: §2.1 Literature search and inclusion criteria (single paragraph)

key_findings.finding: Meta-analysis methods: long-term studies only, run in RevMan 5.2.2 with random-effects models; a domain was pooled when at least three studies reported N, means and SDs on an outcome judged representative; behavioural data from fMRI studies were excluded; standardized mean differences with 95% CIs; I² over 75% taken as high, and a study contributing largely to I² was left out of the pool.
key_findings.locator: §2.2 Outline of the review and analyses, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The 14 acute studies had 8 to 48 participants each (editors' count: 13 of the 14 had 14 or fewer; 183 in total). All participants had previous cocaine experience, described as experienced or recreational use, cocaine dependence or crack use; abstinence before sessions ranged from under 72 hours to weeks; routes were intravenous, oral, intranasal and smoked.
key_findings.note: Doses per study are listed in Table 2 as study conditions and are not reproduced on this card.

key_findings.finding: Acute attention: five studies; the text counts two with no effect, two with impairment and one with improvement and reaches no conclusion.
key_findings.note: Table 2 codes the same studies as one decrease, three no effect and one improvement (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Acute response inhibition: three of four studies (Fillmore et al., 2005, 2006; Garavan et al., 2008; 12 to 14 participants each, people who used crack tested within 72 hours of last use or people with recent use) found better inhibitory performance after cocaine than after placebo; the fourth (Fillmore et al., 2002, 8 participants) is described in the text as a dose-related fall in the probability of inhibiting a response. Three of the four studies share a first author (Fillmore).
Acute memory: three studies found no effect on immediate recall, delayed recall or recognition, and one found no effect on repeated acquisition learning.

Acute psychomotor performance: six DSST studies; four found no effect (smoked, intravenous and oral cocaine in people with cocaine dependence or crack use) and two (Higgins et al., 1990, 1993; 8 participants each) found faster responding after intranasal cocaine; too few reported comparable means and SDs for pooling. The authors attribute the difference to the route.
key_findings.note: Editors' observation from Table 2: the two positive studies are also the only ones in recreational samples, so route and type of use cannot be separated.

key_findings.finding: No placebo-controlled acute study existed for cognitive flexibility, performance monitoring or reward processing.

Long-term sustained attention (CPT hits combined with P300 amplitude): pooled SMD −1.22 (95% CI −1.58 to −0.85), lower in the cocaine groups. The number of pooled studies is not stated; other studies, including the one CPT study without a group difference (Liu et al., 2011), were left out because they contributed too much to heterogeneity.

Long-term attention, narrative: four of eight sustained-attention studies found poorer performance and four did not (three of the null studies used the Trail Making Test, which the authors consider a poor attention measure); four Stroop or five-digit studies found no difference in selective attention; all Cocaine Stroop studies found a stronger attentional bias toward cocaine-related words.
key_findings.locator: §3.1.2 Long-term effects, 1st, 3rd and 5th paragraphs (pp. 4–5) and last paragraph (p. 10)

key_findings.finding: Long-term stop-signal reaction time: of five stop-signal studies (all with longer SSRT in the cocaine group, two not significantly), four reported means and SDs; after leaving out Fillmore and Rush (2002) for heterogeneity, three pooled to SMD 0.50 (95% CI 0.11 to 0.90), longer (poorer) in the cocaine groups.

Long-term failed inhibitions (commission errors on Go/NoGo, IMT and CPT): pooled SMD 0.64 (95% CI 0.44 to 0.84), more errors in the cocaine groups; one study using a composite measure found no difference (Moeller et al., 2010a).
key_findings.note: The text says nine studies were pooled but names eight.

key_findings.finding: Long-term immediate recall (correct recalls on CVLT, LMT or RAVLT): eight studies pooled to SMD −0.46 (95% CI −0.70 to −0.23), fewer items recalled in the cocaine groups; narratively seven studies found poorer and two no different recall.
key_findings.note: One of the seven studies counted as showing poorer recall (Reske, 2010) is coded no effect in Table 3 (p. 7).

key_findings.finding: Long-term working memory (not pooled): five of eight studies found poorer performance, more consistently on visuospatial than on verbal tasks; stimulus–response learning results were mixed and too few to generalize.

Long-term perseverative errors (WCST, reversal learning, IED): three of eight studies were left out for heterogeneity (Colzato et al., 2009a,b; Ersche et al., 2008; Fernandez-Serrano et al., 2012); the remaining five pooled to SMD 0.37 (95% CI 0.17 to 0.57), more perseverative errors in the cocaine groups, called a small effect by the authors.

Long-term performance monitoring (not pooled): two ERP studies found a smaller error-related negativity (one also a smaller Pe), and three behavioural measures showed less adjustment after errors or stop signals; the authors call the domain little studied.

Long-term reward-based decision making: delay-discounting k and IGT net scores from seven studies pooled to SMD 0.53 (95% CI 0.32 to 0.75), poorer in the cocaine groups. Narratively, three studies found steeper delay discounting; among IGT-type studies seven found poorer and four no different performance; three studies from one laboratory found a stronger choice of cocaine-related pictures.
key_findings.note: The text introduces the IGT studies as ten, then lists seven plus four.

key_findings.finding: Long-term psychomotor performance: motor responses (DSST substitutions, finger tapping) from three studies, after leaving out Woicik et al. (2009) for heterogeneity, SMD 0.75 (95% CI 0.46 to 1.04); response latency or completion time from six studies (Hanlon et al., 2010, left out because tested during fMRI), SMD −0.24 (95% CI −0.47 to −0.02); both in the direction of slower performance in the cocaine groups.

Abstinence at testing in the long-term studies ranges from under 72 hours, or cocaine-positive urine at screening, to months or years, and is unknown for several studies; by the editors' count about 23 of the 55 distinct study labels include at least some participants tested within 72 hours of last use or with positive urine.
key_findings.locator: Table 3, abstinence column and footnotes c, d, e and g
key_findings.note: Editors' count: labels such as Moeller 2010a,b and Goldstein 2007a,b counted once; entries of at least 2 or 3 days not counted.

key_findings.finding: The authors' own caveats: acute studies tested people who regularly use cocaine, so acute improvement may only offset pre-existing deficits and could be misleading; long-term group differences can never be interpreted as caused solely by cocaine; abstinence varied; most if not all participants used several drugs; lifestyle and education are major potential confounders.
key_findings.locator: §4.3 Considerations in the interpretation of results, 1st–3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: very few studies per pool, no pooling possible for any acute domain, combining different outcome measures is acknowledged to introduce bias, and no subgroup or moderator analysis by abstinence, history of use or type of use was feasible.
key_findings.locator: §4.4 Limitations of the review, 1st, 3rd and 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors propose cocaine-related atherosclerosis as possibly the primary mechanism of a general impairment; the review analyses no vascular measure.

Recreational use: the authors report preliminary evidence of poorer cognitive flexibility in recreational samples (Colzato et al., 2009a,b) but state that few studies examined recreational use and that it is not yet known whether recreational use affects cognition.
key_findings.locator: §3.4.2 Long-term effects, last paragraph (p. 12); §4.5 Directions for future research, 2nd paragraph (p. 16)

reporting_issues.issue: Fillmore et al. (2002), acute stop-signal study: the text describes a dose-related fall in the probability of inhibiting a response (poorer inhibition), but Table 2 codes the study as improved performance.
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction of one of only four acute response-inhibition studies is uncertain from the review; the primary paper must be read before it is cited either way.

reporting_issues.issue: Stillman et al. (1993), acute attention: the text reports a slight decline in attention over 4 hours after cocaine and counts it among two studies showing impairment, while Table 2 codes it as no effect with faster orienting.
reporting_issues.consequence: The acute attention tally (two null, two impaired, one improved) does not match Table 2 (one decrease, three null, one improved).

reporting_issues.issue: Reske (2010) is counted in the text among seven studies showing poorer immediate recall, but Table 3 codes it as no effect on the CVLT; it is also among the eight studies in the recall pool.
reporting_issues.consequence: The narrative count of positive studies is overstated by at least one; how this study entered the pooled estimate cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: Abi-Saab et al. (2005) is listed in the text among four studies showing psychomotor impairment and enters the motor-response pool, but Table 3 codes its psychomotor tests (DSST, finger tapping, grooved pegboard and others) as no effect.
reporting_issues.consequence: The motor-response pool of only three studies, SMD 0.75, includes a study the table describes as null, after a null study (Woicik et al., 2009) was removed for heterogeneity.

reporting_issues.issue: Counts in the text disagree with the studies named: nine commission-error studies with eight named (p. 10); ten IGT studies, then seven impaired plus four null (p. 13); six response-time studies with seven named (p. 14); working memory introduced as seven studies and summarized as five of eight (p. 11); three of five set-shifting studies supported by four citations (p. 12).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor individually, but the pooled study sets cannot be reconstructed with certainty from the text.

reporting_issues.issue: No I² is reported for any pool although the methods say it was computed, and studies were removed post hoc for their contribution to heterogeneity in four of eight pools (attention, stop-signal, perseveration, motor responses), including null studies; the attention pool's studies are not identified, nor which three stop-signal and five perseveration studies remained; no forest plots, per-study effects or participant totals.
reporting_issues.consequence: The pooled SMDs describe selected subsets with confidence intervals that understate between-study spread; they cannot be checked or reproduced from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The signs of the pooled SMDs are not oriented consistently: poorer performance appears as negative for attention, immediate recall and response time, and as positive for stop-signal reaction time, commission errors, perseveration, decision making and motor responses.
reporting_issues.consequence: Direction must be taken from the text; a claim quoting a sign alone could invert the finding.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 includes two long-term studies published before the 2003 cut-off (Fillmore, 2002; Kirby et al., 1999), and the abstract says all available case-controlled studies were reviewed although long-term studies before 2003 were excluded by design.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the inclusion rule was not applied strictly, and the abstract overstates completeness.

reporting_issues.issue: Study labels in Table 3 carry different sample sizes in different domains: Colzato (2009b) 13 vs 16 and 20 vs 20; Woicik et al. (2011) 107 vs 107 and, under psychomotor performance, 64 vs 64 (the size given for Woicik et al., 2009); van der Plas et al. (2009) 27 vs 36 and 22 vs 21. The text and table also differ on years (Vadhan 2008 vs 2009 for stimulus–response learning; Fernandez-Serrano 2011 vs 2012 for the mood-induction study) and on spelling (Lui vs Liu, 2012).
reporting_issues.consequence: Which primary paper supports a given row is uncertain in several places; primary studies should be identified by DOI before citation.

reporting_issues.issue: The PDF is the uncorrected proof: author queries Q1–Q16 remain, an editing bracket is left in §4.5, an Uncited references list is printed, and Table 2 labels its last section 3.7 instead of 3.8.
reporting_issues.consequence: Some of the errors listed here may have been corrected in the version of record (Neurosci Biobehav Rev 37(8):1838–1859), which was not read.

verification.source_read: Uncorrected proof PDF ('Article in press', Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews xxx (2013) xxx–xxx; 19 pages numbered 1–19, equal to the PDF pages), not the version of record (37(8):1838–1859 in the reference record), so anchors give PDF pages, which differ from the published pagination. All pages read; Tables 1–3 (Table 3 landscape, PDF pp. 6–9) and every number on this card checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi; the paper has no figures; no supplementary material.
